beats: A man is arrested on his birthday, and nobody ever tells him why!
This is The Trial, by Franz Kafka.
Josef K. is a bank officer, and the guards arresting him eat his breakfast!
His first hearing is in a slum tenement, on a Sunday.
He gives a fiery speech, then sees everyone wears court badges!
Then, at his bank, he finds the guards being whipped, because he complained.
Next day he opens the door: same guards, same whip!
His lawyer works from a sickbed and never files a petition.
A court painter has never seen a single real acquittal!
The court has offices in nearly every attic, even behind the painter's bed.
A priest tells him of a man who waits his whole life at a door to the law.
Dying, the man learns the door was meant only for him; now it's shutting.
A year later, two men in top hats walk him to a quarry.
They bring a butcher's knife; his last words: like a dog!
Kafka's point: you don't need to believe the system is true, only necessary.
And nobody ever told him why.
